summary:
Base Commander is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12 in which they run a base on the Moon or on Mars. Every day
the Sun gives them energy and they must choose where it goes: making oxygen for the crew, powering a radiation
shield, saving it in batteries for the long lunar night, or building. There is never a free choice, so children
learn by playing the real trade-offs of surviving in space. What makes it special is that the game is driven by the
real Sun: every solar storm is a real solar flare recorded by NASA's DONKI database, and the more active the real Sun
was this week, the more storms come. It works on phones and computers, in English and Spanish, with no download or
account, and every hard word (radiation dose, sol, solar storm) is explained the moment a child taps it.
details:
What it does. Base Commander turns a space mission into decisions a child can make. Each day (or Martian sol) the player shares out the energy from the solar panels between three things: the oxygen machine (the crew breathes 3 units a day; an empty tank ends the mission), the radiation shield (it blocks solar storms, but only on the day it is powered) and the battery (whatever is left is saved for later, up to its capacity). Players can also spend energy to build or upgrade solar towers, batteries and oxygen tanks, or move them around the base. Energy spent on one thing is not there for another, so every choice is a real trade-off.

Three modes. Escape: the ship crash-lands and its five broken parts are scattered around; the player sends a rover to collect them. Each trip costs energy and suit oxygen and takes one or two days; outside the base there is no shield, and a strong solar storm damages the rover, which comes back late and must be repaired. The crew's food lasts 21 days on the Moon and 18 sols on Mars, so the ship must be repaired and launched before it runs out. Survival: keep the crew safe for 14 days. Infinite: last as long as possible and beat your record, with a world ranking per map and difficulty (no accounts and no personal data: nicknames are picked from word lists). Two maps: the Moon (7 days of sun, then 7 days of dark lunar night with no solar power) and Mars, unlocked by winning on the Moon (less sunlight, dust storms that halve solar power, slower warnings because messages from Earth take minutes, and a lower background dose thanks to its thin air). Three difficulty levels.

How real data drives the game. The game asks NASA's DONKI space-weather database for the latest solar flares when it starts, and keeps a saved library of one year of real flares. Every storm in the game is one of those real flares: its class (C, M or X) sets how strong it is, and the number of big flares the real Sun produced in the last 7 days sets how often storms come. Mission Control warns the base when "scientists saw a flare" (showing the class), and after a storm tells the player which real flare it was and when it happened. A "Real Sun" panel shows this week's flares with a clear LIVE or SAVED label, so saved data is never shown as live. Radiation numbers come from NASA's OSDR RadLab measurements.

How it helps kids learn. Short sentences, tap-to-explain words, a step-by-step tutorial with a read-aloud button and small animations, a daily report that explains what happened and why, and a mission radio between the crew and Mission Control. It works on phones, tablets and computers, in English and Spanish (adding a language is adding one text file), with no download and no account. Players can lose and try again: a short "mission failed" scene and a red end screen explain exactly why (out of oxygen, too much radiation or out of time) and give a tip. Storms change every game, so it is very replayable. The difficulty levels were balanced by simulating hundreds of games for every mode and map.

What we hope to achieve. That children understand why astronauts care about energy, oxygen and radiation, that they connect what they play with the real Sun of today, and that teachers can use it in class in a few minutes.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (a static website on GitHub Pages), three.js for the 3D base, Google Gemini text-to-speech for the voices, Node.js scripts to save the NASA data, Git and GitHub. An AI coding assistant (Claude Code) helped write the code under my direction; the idea and every design decision are mine (details in the README).

Links. Play: https://joelxd18.github.io/junior-astronaut-trainer/ · Code: https://github.com/JoelXD18/junior-astronaut-trainer
dataRefs: DONKI – NASA Space Weather Database (real solar flares that drive every storm in the game)
DONKI web services (live flare data loaded when the game starts)
OSDR RadLab – real radiation dose measurements (ISS, Artemis I, Curiosity, CRaTER)
NASA 3D Resources – Apollo Lunar Module, Habitat Demonstration Unit, Astronaut, Perseverance rover, Earth and Mars maps
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit – LRO/LROC color map of the Moon
Mars 2020 Perseverance – MOXIE oxygen experiment (fact used in the game)
projectRefs: Supabase – database for the Infinite-mode world ranking
Google Gemini text-to-speech – AI voices (radio, tutorial, demo narration)
